meaning: Argues about the price of something to get a better deal
trick: HAGGLE sounds like 'hag-gal': an old lady bargaining hard at the market.
examples: Perhaps we are the only animal that haggles.
My mother always haggles with the vegetable seller.

usage.pattern: haggles over/about something / haggles with someone

meaning: Arguing about the price of something to agree on a deal
trick: HAGGLING = the back-and-forth of a market bargain.
examples: You'll move on to the final act of negotiation: haggling.
After ten minutes of haggling, we got the bag for half price.

meaning: Storms in which small balls of ice fall from the sky
trick: HAIL + STORMS: storms that throw ice balls (ole).
examples: The wind comes in hailstorms.
Heavy hailstorms damaged the farmers' crops.

meaning: Ways of cutting and arranging hair (informal)
trick: HAIR + DO: what you DO with your hair.
examples: I even concocted wild hairdos.
The girls tried new hairdos for the wedding.

usage.pattern: a + adjective + hairdo / try new hairdos

meaning: (Of an old person) strong and healthy
trick: HALE sounds like 'hail and healthy': 'hale and hearty'.
examples: He was still quite hale and hearty, so he took on the keeper's job.
My grandfather is ninety but still hale and hearty.

meaning: A circle of light around something bright; also a ring of light drawn around a holy person's head
trick: HALO = 'hello' from an angel wearing a ring of light.
examples: The orange halo from an explosion lit up the night sky.
The moon had a soft halo around it tonight.

usage.pattern: a halo of light / a halo around something

meaning: A type of very bright electric lamp or light; also a group of chemical elements such as chlorine
hindi: हैलोजन बत्ती, तेज़ रोशनी वाला बल्ब
trick: HALOGEN lamp makes a bright HALO of light.
examples: Fog gathered around the halogen street lights.
We put a halogen lamp in the kitchen for more light.

meaning: Rings or circles, such as rings of smoke or light
trick: HALOS = many little O-shaped rings.
examples: He sat by the window one night, blowing halos of smoke.
The street lamps had misty halos around them in the fog.

usage.pattern: halos of something / halos around something

meaning: Stopped moving or stopped something from continuing
trick: HALTED: the soldier shouted 'HALT!' and he stopped.
examples: Instead of going, he halted behind my chair.
The bus halted suddenly at the red light.

meaning: Hanging beds made of cloth or net, tied between two trees or posts
trick: HAMMOCKS: HAMMER the posts in and hang the swing beds.
examples: For ten days we moved through the jungle, sleeping in hammocks.
We tied two hammocks between the palm trees on the beach.

usage.pattern: sleep in hammocks / hang hammocks between something

meaning: A small number of people or things; also as much as you can hold in one hand
trick: HANDFUL = what fits in a HAND: just a few.
examples: Except for a handful of days, Rasheed didn't keep the fast.
Only a handful of students came to class on Friday.

meaning: A small square of cloth for wiping your nose, face or hands
trick: HAND + KERCHIEF: a little cloth you keep in your hand (say 'HANG-ker-chif').
examples: As I had no hat, I tried to fan myself with my handkerchief.
He wiped his face with a white handkerchief.

meaning: A person who does small repairs and odd jobs in a house or building
trick: HANDY + MAN: a man who is handy with tools.
examples: Tariq was hired as a janitor and handyman.
We called a handyman to fix the leaking tap.

meaning: Doing something that ruins yourself (used figuratively); originally a Japanese ritual suicide by cutting the stomach
trick: HARA-KIRI: Japanese 'hara' (belly) + 'kiri' (cut) - now means wrecking yourself.
examples: Giving that up would be like committing psychological hara-kiri.
Raising prices so much would be business hara-kiri.

meaning: Long, angry speeches or lectures criticising someone
trick: HARANGUE = HARASS with a long angry speech.
examples: All these harangues of accusations kept bouncing in her head.
The coach's harangues after every loss made the team nervous.

meaning: A sign or person that shows something is going to happen soon
trick: HARBINGER = a HERALD who BRINGS news of what's coming.
examples: She said our relationship would be the harbinger of a new age of peace.
Dark clouds are often a harbinger of heavy rain.

meaning: A sheltered area of water where ships stay safely (US spelling; British 'harbour'); also to keep a feeling or secret in your mind
trick: HARBOR = a safe HARBOUR (British) for boats.
examples: So I caught the streetcar that goes down to the harbor.
Many small fishing boats were tied up in the harbor.

usage.pattern: in/at the harbor / harbor a feeling

meaning: Kept a feeling, thought or secret in your mind for a long time (US spelling; British 'harboured'); also gave shelter to someone
trick: HARBORED: like a ship in a harbor, the thought stayed parked in your mind.
examples: For years I'd harbored a suspicion that we all had a limit.
She harbored a secret dream of becoming a singer.

meaning: Tough, aggressive methods used to get what you want (informal); also the sport of baseball
trick: HARDBALL: playing with a HARD BALL - no soft moves.
examples: Some CEOs use hardball tactics to drive down the price.
If they won't pay, we'll have to play hardball.

meaning: A person who holds strict views and refuses to change or compromise, especially in politics or religion
trick: HARD + LINE: someone who never moves from their HARD LINE.
examples: The court was filled with hardliner mullahs who brought in strict laws.
The party chose a hardliner as its new leader.

usage.pattern: a hardliner on something / hardliner + noun

meaning: Situations that are hard to bear, such as lack of money, food or comfort
trick: HARDSHIPS = HARD trips through life.
examples: Until you experience hardships like failure, your mind will remain soft.
My grandparents faced many hardships after the war.

meaning: A small keyboard instrument that makes music by pumping air through reeds
trick: HARMONIUM makes HARMONY - the bhajan box.
examples: Downstairs, someone was tuning a harmonium.
My uncle plays the harmonium at every family puja.

meaning: To control and use something (like power or energy) for a useful purpose; also a set of straps for a horse or a person
hindi: काबू में करके उपयोग करना; जीन, पट्टा
trick: HARNESS: put straps on a wild horse and make it work for you.
examples: I learned how to harness my mind to take more pain.
We can harness the power of the sun to make electricity.

meaning: Kept talking about the same thing again and again in an annoying way (harp on)
hindi: बार-बार वही बात कही, रट लगाई
trick: HARPED: kept plucking the same HARP string again and again.
examples: I couldn't understand why he harped on this point so much.
My mother harped on about my messy room all week.

meaning: Extremely upsetting and painful to experience
trick: HARROWING: like a HARROW (farm tool) dragging across your heart.
examples: All bad things end, no matter how harrowing the pain gets.
They told us about their harrowing journey across the sea.

meaning: Farm tools with metal teeth or discs, pulled over ploughed land to break up the soil
trick: HARROWS: like a row of ARROWS dragged over the field to break the soil.
examples: Electricity could run threshing machines, ploughs and harrows.
The farmer pulled the harrows across the field with a tractor.

meaning: The time or work of cutting and collecting crops; also the crops gathered
trick: HARVEST: in autumn, farmers HAVE their best crops.
examples: The animals went down to the hayfield to begin the harvest.
The village celebrates after the rice harvest.

usage.pattern: begin/bring in the harvest / a good harvest

meaning: Gathered or collected a lot of something (used figuratively); also cut and gathered crops
trick: HARVESTED: picked them up like crops in the field.
examples: That was the bait for quitters, and he harvested helmets left and right.
The farmers harvested the wheat before the rain came.

meaning: A drug made from the resin of the cannabis plant, smoked or eaten
trick: HASHISH: HASH + HUSH - an illegal drug kept hush-hush.
examples: The hashish was hidden in the seams of the coat.
The police found a small packet of hashish in his bag.

meaning: Doing something in a hurry, often too quickly
trick: HASTE: Haste makes waste.
examples: He left the room with wordless haste.
In her haste, she forgot her phone at home.

usage.pattern: in haste / in someone's haste (to do something)

meaning: Thought up or planned something, often secretly; also came out of an egg
hindi: योजना बनाई, सोची; अंडे से निकला
trick: HATCHED: the plan came out of your head like a chick from an egg.
examples: I hatched the plan at Walmart the night before.
The chicks hatched early this morning.

meaning: A very strong feeling of dislike
trick: HATRED = HATE + RED anger.
examples: In that moment my hatred overcame my fear.
There is no place for hatred in our home.

meaning: Behaving as if you are better than others
trick: HAUGHTY = HIGH-ty: nose held high.
examples: Napoleon came out, casting haughty glances from side to side.
The haughty shop owner refused to talk to us.

meaning: A long period of time or effort needed to reach a goal; also an amount of things taken or caught
trick: HAUL: like dragging a heavy load a long way - the long haul.
examples: I've committed to one woman for the long haul.
Learning a language is a long haul, so be patient.

usage.pattern: for the long haul / a long haul

meaning: The back part of the hips and thighs; sitting on them means squatting
trick: HAUNCHES: when you sit on your HAUNCHES you squat low.
examples: He was sitting on his haunches, eating figs from a crate.
The dog sat on its haunches, waiting for food.

meaning: Great damage, confusion and disorder
trick: HAVOC: a storm HAS made a total wreck.
examples: Everything reminded her of the havoc that had struck her life.
The storm caused havoc across the city.

meaning: Making unsure sounds and not deciding, delaying an answer
trick: HAWING: saying 'ha... aw...' when you can't decide.
examples: After hemming and hawing for a bit, he admitted it was his idea.
Stop hemming and hawing and tell me your answer.

meaning: A large bird with sharp eyes that hunts small animals; also a person who supports war
trick: HAWK: HAWK-eye - it sees everything from the sky.
examples: They watched a hawk gliding in circles above the village.
The hawk caught a mouse in the field.

meaning: People who sell things in the street, often calling out loudly
trick: HAWKERS shout like HAWKS to sell their goods.
examples: Cars crawled through the crowd of hawkers and pedestrians.
Hawkers were selling peanuts outside the station.

meaning: Grass that has been cut and dried, used as animal food
trick: HAY: make HAY while the sun shines.
examples: Back to shovelling hay for the horses.
The farmer gave the cows fresh hay.

meaning: A simple person from the countryside (informal, US, often insulting)
trick: HAYSEED: someone with HAY SEEDS still in their hair from the farm.
examples: Back then he was a simple Texas hayseed who barely said a word.
The city boys laughed at him and called him a hayseed.

meaning: Badly wrong or out of control (informal)
trick: HAYWIRE: wire for tying hay gets tangled into a mess.
examples: I wondered how it had all gone so haywire so quickly.
My phone went haywire after the update.

meaning: Something that could be dangerous or cause harm
trick: HAZARD: HAZARD lights warn of danger ahead.
examples: That's a hazard that comes with my line of work.
Wet floors are a hazard in the kitchen.

usage.pattern: a hazard to someone / a fire/health hazard

meaning: A confused state of mind where you can't think clearly; also thin mist, smoke or dust in the air
trick: HAZE: a HAZY mist over your mind or the sky.
examples: She kept talking, trying to reach me through the haze of pain.
There was a light haze over the hills this morning.

usage.pattern: through a haze / a haze of something

meaning: Of a light greenish-brown colour, used for eyes
trick: HAZEL: like a hazelnut - light brown.
examples: She saw her own reflection in his hazel eyes.
The baby has big hazel eyes like her father.

meaning: To listen carefully (old-fashioned/poetic)
trick: HEARKEN: has 'HEAR' inside it.
examples: Beasts of every land, hearken to my joyful tidings.
Hearken, children, to the old man's story.

meaning: A vehicle that carries a dead body in a coffin to a funeral
trick: HEARSE has 'HEAR' + 'SE' - all you hear at a funeral is silence.
examples: The warden said that the hearse had arrived.
A black hearse drove slowly to the cemetery.

meaning: Causing great sadness and emotional pain
trick: HEART + WRENCH: a story that twists your heart like a wrench.
examples: Readers called the book inspiring and heart-wrenching.
The film had a heart-wrenching ending.

meaning: Causing great sadness and pity
trick: HEART + REND (tear): a story that tears your heart.
examples: The reviewer said the novel was just as heartrending as the first.
We heard a heartrending cry from the next room.

meaning: A serious illness caused by staying too long in great heat
trick: HEAT + STROKE: the heat strikes you down.
examples: If you go too slowly, there's the risk of heatstroke.
Drink water in summer so you don't get heatstroke.

meaning: Rose and fell heavily, as when breathing hard; also let out (a sigh) or lifted something heavy
trick: HEAVED: a HEAVY up-and-down.
examples: My lungs heaved after the long run.
She heaved a sigh of relief when the exam ended.

usage.pattern: someone's chest/lungs heaved / heave a sigh

meaning: Sure to go to heaven after death
trick: HEAVEN + BOUND (headed for): on the road to heaven.
examples: My father was a dear man, surely heaven-bound.
Grandma was so kind that everyone said she was heaven-bound.

meaning: Rising and falling heavily, as when breathing hard; also very crowded (British informal)
trick: HEAVING: chest going up and down HEAVILY.
examples: At mile eighteen I was bonking, my lungs heaving.
He reached the top of the stairs, his chest heaving.

meaning: A very loud kind of rock music with strong guitars and drums
hindi: हेवी मेटल संगीत, तेज़ रॉक संगीत
trick: HEAVY METAL: music as loud as heavy metal banging.
examples: Mustaine is one of the most influential musicians in heavy-metal music.
My brother listens to heavy-metal music all day.

meaning: Rude shouts or interruptions aimed at a speaker or performer
trick: HECKLES: people HECK-ling you from the crowd.
examples: There were heckles and jeers from the crowd.
The comedian ignored the heckles and kept going.

meaning: Avoided giving a clear answer or decision; also protected against loss
trick: HEDGED: hid behind a HEDGE instead of answering.
examples: Aziza hedged, stiff with embarrassment.
When I asked about the money, he hedged.

meaning: Rows of bushes growing close together, forming a border
trick: HEDGES: green walls along the edges of a garden.
examples: Lump sugar and linseed cake grew on the hedges.
My father trims the hedges every Sunday.

meaning: Paying attention to advice or a warning and acting on it
trick: HEEDING: HEAD-ing the advice - keeping it in your head.
examples: What will be my defense for not heeding His commands?
He drove fast, not heeding the warning signs.

meaning: Not paying attention to something; not caring about danger or results
trick: HEED-LESS: no heed, no care.
examples: They fired rockets, heedless of the innocent people who would die.
He ran into the road, heedless of the traffic.

meaning: Big and strong, or heavy and powerful
trick: HEFTY: so HEAVY you need to lift (heft) it.
examples: A hefty gust of wind could send you sailing off.
He paid a hefty fine for parking there.

meaning: Made stronger or greater (often used for feelings or senses)
trick: HEIGHTENED: raised to a greater HEIGHT.
examples: Now cooking was an exercise in heightened anxiety.
There is heightened security at the airport today.

meaning: A valuable object passed down in a family for many years
trick: HEIRLOOM: something an HEIR gets from the family.
examples: They would value their difficulties as one would a family heirloom.
This gold ring is a family heirloom.

meaning: Careless enough to break precious family objects (made-up compound used as an insult)
trick: HEIRLOOM + BREAKING: the clumsy child who smashes grandma's vase.
examples: "An heirloom-breaking, clumsy little brat," she muttered.
My heirloom-breaking puppy knocked Grandma's vase off the table.

meaning: Extremely difficult or unpleasant (US informal); also extremely good or impressive
trick: HELL + -ACIOUS: as tough as hell.
examples: Another hellacious special forces school put us through so much.
We drove home through a hellacious storm.

meaning: Hard hats worn to protect the head
trick: HELMETS protect the HELM (top) of your head.
examples: He collected the helmets of quitters left and right.
Riders must wear helmets on the bike.

meaning: The bottom edge of a piece of clothing, folded and sewn; also (verb) to sew such an edge
trick: HEM: the very edge - 'hem-line' at the bottom.
examples: She practiced walking in it and kept stepping on the hem.
My mother took up the hem of my trousers.

usage.pattern: the hem of something / take up a hem

meaning: Not deciding or speaking clearly, making unsure sounds before answering; also sewing an edge
trick: HEMMING: 'hmm... hmm...' when you can't make up your mind.
examples: After hemming and hawing for a bit, he admitted it was his idea.
She kept hemming and hawing about which dress to buy.

meaning: Lost a large amount of something (like money or time) fast (US spelling; British 'haemorrhaged'); also bled heavily
hindi: तेज़ी से गँवाया; बहुत ख़ून बहा
trick: HEMORRHAGED: like heavy bleeding - it just poured away.
examples: I hemorrhaged time.
The company hemorrhaged money last year.

meaning: A reddish-brown dye from a plant, used to colour hands, hair or nails
trick: HENNA = HINA, the mehndi at every wedding.
examples: Her palms were painted red with henna.
The bride had beautiful henna patterns on her hands.

meaning: Is a sign that something is coming; announces something
hindi: संकेत देता है, घोषणा करता है
trick: HERALDS: the HERALD (royal messenger) announces what's coming.
examples: Each new piece of information heralds a step forward.
The first cold wind heralds the arrival of winter.

meaning: A plant whose leaves are used in cooking or medicine
trick: HERB: HERBal tea is made from these leaves.
examples: On the way, Mariam saw herb shops and fruit stalls.
Mint is my favourite herb for chutney.

meaning: Large groups of animals (or people) that move together
trick: HERDS: you HEAR the herds coming before you see them.
examples: Villages turned into herds of nomadic people, always moving.
Herds of cattle grazed by the river.

meaning: People who live alone, away from others, often for religious reasons
trick: HERMITS live in a HERMIT crab's shell - all alone.
examples: Five thousand monks once lived as hermits in these caves.
The old man lives like a hermit in the hills.

meaning: Slow to act or speak because you are unsure or worried
trick: HESITANT: HESITATES before every step.
examples: For the first time, he was hesitant.
She was hesitant to ask for help.

usage.pattern: be hesitant to do something / about something

meaning: Very ugly or very unpleasant; shocking
trick: HIDEOUS: so ugly you want to HIDE from it.
examples: The animals were treated with hideous cruelty.
She wore a hideous green hat to the party.

meaning: The skins of animals, used for leather; also (verb) keeps out of sight
trick: HIDES: the animal's skin HIDES its body.
examples: The Vikings camped in tents made of deer hides.
They made shoes from cow hides.

meaning: Short periods of great pleasure or excitement; also high points or top temperatures
trick: HIGHS and lows: the ups of life.
examples: Highs are shallow and unproductive ways to go about one's life.
Every job has its highs and lows.

usage.pattern: highs and lows / the highs of something

meaning: Great amusement and loud laughter
trick: HILARITY: things are HILARIOUS - everyone laughs.
examples: He saw them as a cousin prone to acts of hilarity and scandal.
The dog chasing its tail caused great hilarity.

meaning: Completely, all the way (used after 'to the'); also the handle of a sword or knife
trick: HILT: push a sword in up to the HILT - all the way.
examples: "I can prove this to the hilt, gentlemen of the jury."
He has borrowed money up to the hilt.

meaning: At the back (used for animals' legs)
trick: HIND = beHIND: the legs at the back.
examples: No animal could stand on his hind legs.
The horse stood up on its hind legs.

meaning: The back part of an animal, including its back legs
trick: HIND + QUARTERS: the back quarter of an animal.
examples: Four large rats were sitting on their hindquarters, listening.
The cow kicked with its hindquarters.

meaning: Things that make it difficult to do something or make progress
trick: HINDRANCES HINDER you - they get in the way.
examples: They are not to blame for their problems and hindrances.
Lack of money and time were the main hindrances to her studies.

meaning: Understanding a situation only after it has happened
trick: HIND = behind: SIGHT looking behind you, at the past.
examples: In hindsight, I could see the warning signs I had chosen to ignore.
In hindsight, we should have left home earlier.

usage.pattern: in hindsight / with hindsight / with the benefit of hindsight

meaning: To depend completely on something; also to be fixed on a moving joint
hindi: पर निर्भर होना; कब्जे से जुड़ा होना
trick: A door turns on its HINGE; your future turns (depends) on this.
examples: At some point your career and finances all hinge on your ability to negotiate.
Our trip will hinge on the weather.

usage.pattern: something hinges on something / be hinged to something

meaning: Metal joints on which a door, gate or lid swings open and shut
trick: HINGES make a door swing - 'hinge' sounds like 'swing'.
examples: She knew how far her door would open before its hinges creaked.
Dad oiled the gate hinges to stop the squeaking.

usage.pattern: the hinges of a door / on its hinges

meaning: A person who rejects normal society, often with long hair, loose clothes and peaceful ideas (1960s style)
trick: HIPPIE: hip, happy, peace-and-love drifter of the 1960s.
examples: Suzuki was an adventurer, an explorer, and a bit of a hippie.
My uncle was a hippie who travelled around India in a van.

usage.pattern: a bit of a hippie / an old hippie

meaning: Making a long 'sss' sound like a snake or angry cat; also of steam or air escaping
trick: Say it slowly - hiSSSSing is the sound itself.
examples: I opened the dumpster lid and found a live raccoon, hissing mad.
The cat arched its back, hissing at the dog.

usage.pattern: hissing at someone / hissing with anger

meaning: Informal: to go to bed to sleep
trick: Old beds were sacks of straw - you 'hit' (fall onto) the sack.
examples: After dinner I'd ride for two more hours, then hit the sack.
I'm so tired, I'm going to hit the sack early.

meaning: To get a free ride in someone's vehicle; also to tie or attach something (e.g. your hopes) to something
trick: HITCH-hiking: hitch a ride with your thumb up.
examples: In Afghanistan we hitch rides with the Army.
She hitched a ride to town with her neighbour.

usage.pattern: hitch a ride with someone / hitch something to something

meaning: Travelling by getting free rides from passing drivers
trick: HITCH a ride + HIKING: walking and thumbing lifts.
examples: He spent four years hitchhiking his way across Asia and Africa.
Hitchhiking can be unsafe at night.

usage.pattern: go hitchhiking / hitchhike your way across somewhere

meaning: Sounding rough and low, often from shouting or a sore throat
trick: HOARSE sounds like HORSE - you sound like a horse after shouting.
examples: I'd scream into a pillow until I was hoarse.
Her voice was hoarse after the cricket match.

usage.pattern: be/go hoarse / a hoarse voice / shout yourself hoarse

meaning: Walked with difficulty and pain, as if injured
trick: HOBBLE ~ wobble: walking wobbly on a hurt leg.
examples: Swollen and sore, I pulled myself out of bed and hobbled into work.
He hobbled to the car on his twisted ankle.

meaning: The act of lifting something up, especially with ropes (like a flag)
trick: HOIST = raise up high, like the flag on Independence Day.
examples: First came the hoisting of the flag.
The students watched the hoisting of the flag at school.

usage.pattern: the hoisting of something / hoisting something up

meaning: To manage to keep a job for a long time
trick: HOLD it DOWN so it doesn't fly away - keep the job steady.
examples: He couldn't hold down a job.
She managed to hold down two jobs while studying.

usage.pattern: hold down a job / can't hold down a job

meaning: People who keep resisting or refusing to give in when others have stopped
hindi: अड़े रहने वाले, न झुकने वाले
trick: They HOLD OUT against the others - they won't give up.
examples: These holdouts continued to fight as they had before.
Only a few holdouts still refuse to use smartphones.

usage.pattern: the last holdouts / holdouts against something

meaning: Informal, mainly US: shouted loudly
trick: HOLLER ~ hollow-er: shouting so loud it echoes.
examples: My mom pulled up alongside me and hollered, "You are two minutes off the lead!"
She hollered at the kids to come in for dinner.

meaning: Without real meaning or sincerity; also empty inside, or a small dip in a surface
trick: A HOLLOW drum is empty inside - hollow words are empty too.
examples: She could hear the insincerity beneath his hollow, false assurances.
His promises sounded hollow to the voters.

usage.pattern: hollow words/promises / ring hollow / the hollow of something

meaning: Sad because you are away from your home and family
trick: HOME + SICK: sick with missing home.
examples: She sat on the bed, missing her mother, feeling homesick.
In his first week at hostel he felt very homesick.

meaning: The crime of killing a person
trick: HOMO = human + -CIDE = kill (like pesticide).
examples: We are not concerned with a homicide committed on a sudden impulse.
The police are treating his death as a homicide.

usage.pattern: commit homicide / an act of homicide

meaning: Sharpens or improves a skill or ability; also sharpens a blade
trick: HONE rhymes with STONE - a sharpening stone hones a knife.
examples: Commitment hones your attention and focus.
Daily practice hones her singing skills.

usage.pattern: something hones something / hone your skills

meaning: A climbing plant with sweet-smelling yellow or white flowers
trick: Kids SUCK the sweet HONEY nectar from its flowers.
examples: There was honeysuckle growing along the path.
The honeysuckle on the fence smells lovely in the evening.

usage.pattern: honeysuckle grows / the smell of honeysuckle

meaning: Informal: a poor city neighbourhood; also the metal cover over a car engine (US), or a head covering on a jacket
trick: 'hood = short for neighbourHOOD.
examples: By nineteen he was living on his own in the hood.
She ran her fingers along the hood of his shiny car.

usage.pattern: in the hood / the hood of a car

meaning: The hard foot of a horse, cow, goat and similar animals
trick: HOOF goes 'hoof-hoof' like a galloping horse sound.
examples: He would trace the letters in the dust with his great hoof.
The horse lifted its hoof so the blacksmith could clean it.

usage.pattern: an animal's hoof / on the hoof

meaning: A nose that curves down in the middle, like a hook or beak
trick: A nose shaped like a fishing HOOK.
examples: In the mirror she saw his big square face and his hooked nose.
The old man in the story had a long, hooked nose.

usage.pattern: have a hooked nose / a man with a hooked nose

meaning: Laughed or shouted loudly, often to mock; also made an owl or car-horn sound
trick: HOOT like an owl - or like 'hooting' a speaker in an Indian college.
examples: At this, the boys hooted even harder.
The crowd hooted when the player missed the easy catch.

usage.pattern: hoot at someone / hoot with laughter

meaning: Making loud shouts or calls, often in excitement or fun
trick: HOOTING - like students hooting in a college fest.
examples: She saw street children hooting and giving chase.
Fans were hooting and clapping as the team arrived.

usage.pattern: hooting and something / hooting at someone

meaning: Loud shouts of laughter or mockery
trick: HOOTS of laughter - like owls hooting at night.
examples: She lay in bed as the hoots and laughter downstairs grew louder.
His silly joke was met with hoots of laughter.

usage.pattern: hoots of laughter / hoots from someone

meaning: Plural of hoof: the hard feet of horses, donkeys, cows, etc.
trick: One HOOF, many HOOVES (like roof → rooves in old English).
examples: Donkeys slog along, their hooves splattering mud from the puddles.
We heard the horses' hooves on the road.

usage.pattern: the hooves of something / sound of hooves

meaning: Got on or into something quickly; also jumped on one foot
trick: HOP on the bus - quick little jump.
examples: He hopped on the saddle and rode back to Herat.
She hopped into the car and drove off.

meaning: Moving quickly from place to place; also a children's game of hopping into squares
hindi: इधर-उधर उछलना; लंगड़ी टांग का खेल
trick: HOP across the SCOTCH (scratched) lines of the squares.
examples: I bounced back and forth across countries in a game of global hopscotch.
The girls drew squares on the ground to play hopscotch.

usage.pattern: play hopscotch / a game of hopscotch

meaning: A large, noisy crowd of people
trick: HORDE sounds like 'herd' - a herd of people.
examples: The cars crawled through the horde of hawkers and pedestrians.
A horde of fans rushed to the stage.

usage.pattern: a horde of people / hordes of something

meaning: The line far away where the land or sea seems to meet the sky
trick: HORIZON - the HORIZONtal line far away.
examples: Hundreds of beige lockers stretched away to the horizon.
The sun slowly sank below the horizon.

meaning: So amazing that it goes beyond your usual limits of experience
trick: Breaching (breaking through) your HORIZON - the edge of what you know.
examples: My life was full of fantastic, horizon-breaching experiences.
Travelling alone was a horizon-breaching adventure for her.

meaning: Large wasps with a painful sting
trick: HORNETS have HORNS? No - but a sting that hurts like one.
examples: Two hornets were buzzing overhead, against the skylight.
Don't disturb that nest - it's full of hornets.

usage.pattern: a nest of hornets / stir up a hornets' nest

meaning: Very bad or unpleasant
trick: HORRor-IBLE - like a horror movie: awful.
examples: The movie made me feel horrible, but I loved it because it felt real.
I had a horrible headache all day.

meaning: Filled someone with shock and disgust
trick: HORROR-ified: turned into a horror show.
examples: He drove through the village, and what he saw horrified him.
We were horrified by the news of the accident.

usage.pattern: something horrifies someone / be horrified by/at something

meaning: A small snack served before the main meal
hindi: भोजन से पहले का नाश्ता, स्टार्टर
trick: French: 'outside the work' (main dish); say 'or-DURV'.
examples: While waiting for the hors d'oeuvre, she added up the bill in advance.
Waiters served hors d'oeuvres before dinner.

usage.pattern: serve an hors d'oeuvre / hors d'oeuvres before dinner

meaning: U-shaped iron pieces nailed to horses' hooves; also a lucky symbol
trick: Literally SHOES for a HORSE.
examples: The blacksmith heated the horseshoes until they glowed red.
Some people hang horseshoes over the door for luck.

usage.pattern: nail on horseshoes / a lucky horseshoe

meaning: Sprayed someone or something with water from a hose
trick: HOSE = garden pipe; HOSED = sprayed with it.
examples: The instructors hosed us down with freezing water.
He hosed the mud off his bike.

usage.pattern: hose someone/something down / hose something off

meaning: Unfriendly and ready to fight; also belonging to an enemy
trick: HOSTILE sounds like 'hostel' - a hostile hostel where nobody is friendly.
examples: It was torture knowing he might be alone in hostile territory.
The crowd became hostile when the match was cancelled.

usage.pattern: be hostile to/towards someone / a hostile + noun

meaning: Unfriendly or angry feelings or behaviour towards someone
trick: HOSTILE + -ITY = the feeling of being hostile.
examples: The farm's owners were regarded with hostility by their neighbours.
There was open hostility between the two families.

meaning: Informal: a very successful, confident and skilful person
trick: A HOT SHOT in basketball - always scores.
examples: The class was full of brilliant Harvard students and hotshot students from other top universities.
He thinks he's a hotshot lawyer now.

meaning: To keep troubling or chasing someone for a long time; also a hunting dog
hindi: लगातार सताना, पीछा करना; शिकारी कुत्ता
trick: A HOUND (hunting dog) chases you and won't stop.
examples: The ailments that would hound her for the rest of her days began.
Reporters hound the actor wherever he goes.

usage.pattern: something hounds someone / hound someone for something

meaning: Looking or behaving like a hunting dog
trick: HOUND + LIKE: like a long-faced dog.
examples: His face was long and triangular, a bit houndlike.
The old detective had a sad, houndlike face.

usage.pattern: a houndlike + noun / a bit houndlike

meaning: Dogs used for hunting; (figurative) things that chase you
trick: Hounds HOUND (chase) their prey.
examples: Eventually the hounds of Hell gave up and loped off.
The hounds chased the fox across the field.

usage.pattern: a pack of hounds / the hounds of something

meaning: Small, dirty, poorly built houses
trick: HOVEL ~ hut + shovel: dug-out huts.
examples: The wind lifted kites flown from the roofs of mud hovels.
Many families lived in hovels near the railway line.

meaning: A long, loud cry of pain, sadness or anger
trick: A wolf's HOWL - aaa-OOO.
examples: She ran down the hallway, holding back a howl.
We heard the howl of a wolf at night.

usage.pattern: let out a howl / a howl of pain/protest

meaning: Cried out long and loudly in pain or sadness; also of wind or animals
trick: HOW-L: 'how could this happen!' she howled.
examples: She howled with pain as he slammed the door shut.
The baby howled all night.

usage.pattern: howl with pain/laughter / howl at someone

meaning: Crying loudly in pain, grief or anger
trick: HOWLING like a wolf in pain.
examples: Laila turned around and, howling, ran home.
The child was howling because he lost his toy.

meaning: A loud confused noise of many people talking
trick: HUB-BUB: babble-babble of a busy hub.
examples: Through the door came voices, shouts and chairs scraping - a vague hubbub.
The hubbub of the market woke me up.

usage.pattern: the hubbub of something / amid the hubbub

meaning: Too much pride or self-confidence, which often leads to failure
trick: HUBRIS = 'hub' of 'risk' - too proud, so you crash.
examples: The toll of hubris is heavy, and my bill had come due.
His hubris made him ignore the advice of his coach.

usage.pattern: an act of hubris / the hubris of someone

meaning: Crowding close together, usually to keep warm or feel safe
trick: HUDDLE like players in a team huddle.
examples: We stood in our boat crews, huddling tight to get warm.
The puppies were huddling together in the cold.

meaning: Breathed out loudly from effort or annoyance
trick: HUFF and PUFF - the big bad wolf.
examples: She limped and huffed her way across the clearing.
He huffed and puffed up the stairs.

usage.pattern: huff and puff / huff your way somewhere

meaning: A loud noise or fuss made by many people
trick: HULLA-BALOO sounds like a noisy shout itself.
examples: Three days later there was a terrible hullabaloo.
There was a big hullabaloo over the new parking rules.

usage.pattern: a hullabaloo over/about something / cause a hullabaloo

meaning: The main bodies of ships or boats
trick: HULL sounds like 'hole' - the boat's hull must have no hole!
examples: The tide sloshed against the hulls of the sailboats.
Workers painted the hulls of the old fishing boats.

usage.pattern: the hull of a ship / against the hulls

meaning: A low, steady, continuous sound
trick: HMMMM - the hum is the sound itself.
examples: The air was throbbing with the hum of insects.
I could hear the hum of the fridge at night.

meaning: Concerned with helping people who are suffering
trick: HUMANITARIAN - helping HUMANs in need.
examples: Afghans were crossing into Pakistan by proving humanitarian grounds.
The charity sends humanitarian aid to flood victims.

meaning: Boring and ordinary, with no excitement
trick: HUM-DRUM: humming the same drum beat every day.
examples: The vast majority of life resides in the humdrum middle.
He wanted to escape his humdrum office job.

meaning: Did what someone wanted to keep them happy (US spelling; British 'humoured')
trick: HUMOR them = keep them in a good humour.
examples: At first, Rasheed humored Laila and went with them to the orphanage.
She humored her grandfather by listening to his old stories.

meaning: A small rounded raised shape; also the lump on a camel's back
trick: Camel's HUMP - a round bump.
examples: The small black hump of rock came into view far down the beach.
The car slowed down over the speed hump.

usage.pattern: a hump of something / a speed hump

meaning: Informal (military): marching while carrying a heavy load; also rude slang for having sex
trick: HUMP the load on your back like a camel's hump.
examples: We were humping through the jungle in the dead of night.
The soldiers spent the day humping heavy packs up the hill.

usage.pattern: hump through/up somewhere / hump something somewhere

meaning: Sitting or standing with the back bent and shoulders pulled forward
trick: HUNCH-back: back curled up.
examples: I saw the old men sleeping hunched up on their chairs.
He sat hunched up over his phone.

meaning: Crouched or squatted low; (figurative) settled in to wait or hide
trick: HUNKER DOWN - get low like a hunk of rock.
examples: We need to trust the person hunkered down with us.
He hunkered down and held her for a long time.

usage.pattern: hunker down / be hunkered down somewhere

meaning: A problem or difficulty to overcome; also a barrier jumped in a race
trick: Athletes jump over HURDLES - problems to jump over.
examples: My failing hands presented a big mental hurdle.
Money is the biggest hurdle to starting a business.

usage.pattern: a hurdle to something / overcome/clear a hurdle

meaning: Thrown or shouted with force (insults, abuse, objects)
trick: HURLED ~ hurt-led: thrown to hurt.
examples: Insults were hurled.
He hurled the ball across the field.

meaning: A very strong storm with violent winds; (figurative) a huge rush of something
trick: HURRICANE - wind in a HURRY.
examples: I still wanted to fight through another hurricane of pain.
The hurricane destroyed many houses near the coast.

usage.pattern: a hurricane of something / hit by a hurricane

meaning: Very strong storms with violent winds; (figurative) big effects
trick: HURRICANES - winds in a HURRY.
examples: What hurricanes will you leave in your wake?
Hurricanes often hit Florida in the autumn.

meaning: A sudden or peaceful silence
trick: HUSH - 'shhh!'
examples: She noticed a drowsy hush overtaking Kabul.
A hush fell over the room when the teacher walked in.

meaning: Empty burnt or broken outer remains; also the dry outer covering of seeds
trick: Corn HUSKS - the empty shell left behind.
examples: There were the charred, mangled husks of cars everywhere.
We peeled the husks off the corn.

meaning: Low and rough-sounding (of a voice or sound)
trick: HUSKY voice - dry like a husk.
examples: She could only make a husky, choking sound.
He has a deep, husky voice.

meaning: A pipe in the street that firefighters connect hoses to
trick: HYDRA = water: a HYDRANT gives water.
examples: Dobbs was short and built like a fire hydrant.
Don't park in front of the fire hydrant.

meaning: Worked by the pressure of water or oil
trick: HYDRA = water: powered by liquid pressure.
examples: When she reached the hydraulic doors, she heard him behind her.
The truck uses a hydraulic lift.

meaning: Breathing too fast and deeply, often from panic
trick: HYPER (too much) + VENTILATING (air in-out).
examples: She was hyperventilating.
He started hyperventilating before the exam.

meaning: Saying one thing but doing another
trick: HYPOCRITE: a critic who does the same thing himself.
examples: It seems hypocritical, perverse.
It's hypocritical to tell others not to lie when you lie yourself.

usage.pattern: it is hypocritical to do something / be hypocritical

meaning: Having a dangerously low body temperature
trick: HYPO (under) + THERMIC (heat): heat below normal.
examples: After hours in the waves, we were already borderline hypothermic.
The lost climber was hypothermic when they found him.

meaning: Ideas or guesses that need to be tested (plural of hypothesis)
trick: HYPO-THESES: many 'theses' still under test.
examples: Our values are our hypotheses: this behavior is good; that one is not.
The scientists tested three hypotheses.
